"Even with zero Primary 1 classes, we still have to become a deluxe version of an estate school"

Before the merger takes place, S.K.H. Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School has adopted a "counter-cyclical" approach. Principal Kwong Ka-man said that in the new school year, the school will invest HK$1.8 million to enrich students' diverse learning experiences. The school football pitch will be opened for students to ride bicycles, and the school will also offer free enhanced athletics training, sponsor all students to learn swimming, and strengthen the English curriculum.

The principal said: "Even with zero Primary 1 classes, we still have to create the most wonderful school and become a deluxe version of an estate school." This HK$1.8 million in funding mainly comes from Education Bureau subsidies, school reserves, and donations.

On the first day of school, students who had just moved up a grade had mixed feelings. A student named Wu, knowing that the school had not recruited enough students and that the school would close, said: "I have both happy and unhappy feelings." "I'm happy because in the future there may be more students and it will be more lively; I'm unhappy because it's hard to bear that such a big school would just be gone."

Most memorable is the 'Kei Tak' classroom

Recalling her days at Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School, Wu said the most memorable experience was the exchange tour to Xi'an with teachers and students. Another student named Wong described how teachers would "teach through play," using games to help students learn. She hopes that the Wong Tai Sin school will have teachers as good as those at Kei Tak, and said that what she will miss most is the 'Kei Tak' classroom, "because of the friends there." A student named Tse said: "After studying at Kei Tak for several years, suddenly it's gone — it's a bit sad."

Resources can be concentrated on existing students

Parents' feelings are equally complex. Ms. Au, whose child is in Primary 6, said she felt "a bit sad" upon receiving the news of zero classes, and was also shocked. She said: "The principal has just taken office, and the school has been working very hard. Yet this year, 15 primary schools are facing school closure." She noted that the home-school and teaching team relationship has been nurtured for a long time, and everyone quickly adjusted, saying, "actually there are gains and losses," and "since it is God's arrangement," they instead saw their children become more positive in the face of adversity. The school can also concentrate its resources on existing students and no longer be held hostage by enrolment issues.

"Why should schools be forced to merge just because they can't recruit students?"

Mrs. Wu has a child in Primary 4 and another son who has already graduated. She said her child felt the school had "much more care" when returning to school, and really liked the teachers and principal. "At first, upon receiving the news (of school closure), I was really a bit lost," she said. "Such a good school, why should it be forced to merge just because it can't recruit students?" What she appreciates most about Kei Tak is that it gives children confidence, which is "very much lacking in children nowadays" — her child isn't afraid of everything.

Concerned about cross-district schooling in the future

Mrs. Wong has children in Primary 4 and Primary 6. She frankly said she was definitely unhappy at first, feeling "it wasn't worth it." Mrs. Wong said: "The school is so good, the children learn so happily, why don't other people know about it?" After adjusting her mindset, she believes "there's opportunity in every danger." The merger "may not be the best outcome," but from March this year until now, she has seen the school invite all teachers and students to walk this path together, and the children have learned to face difficulties and challenges together. She is grateful for the close home-school relationship at Kei Tak, saying "we are not fighting alone."

Mrs. Chung, who lives near the school, is more concerned about cross-district schooling in the future. She said the most ideal situation would, of course, be to stay at Kei Tak, as "we all live relatively close," and it only takes a five to ten-minute walk to get to school normally. After the merger plan was announced, she took a bus to inspect the school in Wong Tai Sin and felt she "could accept it," with a bus ride of about 20 minutes, followed by a walk.

Strong sense of belonging to 'Kei Tak'

She once asked her daughter if she wanted to transfer to another primary school in the same district. The daughter said: "I don't want to leave this school," showing a strong sense of belonging to 'Kei Tak.' Mrs. Chung respects her child's choice and will accompany her through it. The school mentioned that there might be school bus and uniform subsidies, but the details have not been finalised. Mrs. Chung said that going cross-district to Wong Tai Sin might mean more school network choices for secondary school placement afterwards, "take it as an opportunity for her to step out of this district." She also mentioned that class sizes are currently very small, and after moving to Wong Tai Sin, class sizes may be larger, requiring readjustment. However, she believes her daughter has already learned to be independent at Kei Tak, so she is "not that worried."

Principal: Focus on doing well in the future

Principal Kwong Ka-man, herself an alumna, frankly said that having zero classes "is not good news for a school," but the key is how to transform it: "We focus on doing well in the future." She does not wish to tell a tragic story, saying "in fact, we are all very positive." The news is not new today, and teachers and students have had time to digest it.

After the Primary 6 graduates leave, Kei Tak has 121 students this school year, and has admitted six transfer students: one in Primary 2, four in Primary 5, and one in Primary 6. Kwong Ka-man said the overall attrition rate for Primary 2 to 6 is similar to previous years, with about ten students leaving during the summer, two of whom had to relocate, and the rest transferred to other districts.

Formerly the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak a.m. school

Asked whether the merger news "scared away" students, she said it cannot be generalised. She pointed out that the Sai Kung District secondary school net is ultimately less attractive than Kwun Tong or "the other side of the harbour." "When there aren't enough students across the whole territory, it's like musical chairs going round and round." Some parents, even before leaving, still expressed confidence in the school, saying they just wanted to study in another district.

The predecessor of 'Kei Tak' was the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak a.m. school. In 2004, the government allocated the Tseung Kwan O school premises, and the two schools split into whole-day schools. Kwong Ka-man said the school in Wong Tai Sin "is actually our alma mater," from the same sponsoring body and the same origin, making the merger relatively easier to handle. Over the next three years, the school will gradually increase joint activities for students from both schools, collaborative lesson preparation, and teaching research, to make it easier for students who need to transfer after three years to adjust.

Allocation follows the Wong Tai Sin school net after graduation

The Education Bureau provides up to HK$1 million in配套 for each merger case, and details such as school bus subsidies are still being finalised. She admitted that some parents find the distance too far and want to stay in Tseung Kwan O; but from another perspective, after graduation, allocation follows the Wong Tai Sin school net, which may offer options such as Kowloon City. Most parents are currently in a state of "cautious观望".

Among the 15 schools with zero Primary 1 classes, eight will be merged, including S.K.H. Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School and S.K.H. Kei Tak Primary School in Wong Tai Sin, which will merge across districts, with completion expected in the 2029-2030 school year. In addition, four will cease operation, two will operate private Primary 1 classes, and one will continue to participate in Primary 1 allocation.
